subject: ba
title: Business Social Responsibility
objectives: Define Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) and trace its historical evolution.
Analyse the dimensions of CSR: Economic, Legal, Ethical and Discretionary.
Evaluate the arguments for and against CSR.
Understand the stakeholder concept (primary vs secondary) and contemporary CSR issues.
study:
Bowen (1953) first defined social responsibility as the set of moral and personal obligations an employer must follow, weighing decisions against society's objectives and values. ISO 26000 defines it as an organisation's responsibility for the impact of its decisions and activities on society and the environment, through transparent, ethical behaviour. The idea is commonly summarised as the Triple Bottom Line: profit, people, planet.

Key termCorporate Social Responsibility — a strategic approach to business management that extends beyond isolated charitable giving, integrating social and environmental concerns into how a company actually operates.

The term 'CSR' has been in wide use only since the 1960s, though expectations of responsible business conduct go back further. Late-19th-century 'Social Darwinism' justified cutthroat, brutal competition with little concern for social impact; a backlash began around 1900, exemplified by the Sherman Antitrust Act, and business gradually accepted responsibilities beyond pure profit and legal compliance through the 20th century.

Carroll and Buchholtz's (2003) four-part definition remains the standard framework, often visualised as a pyramid: Economic responsibility (be profitable — the foundation), Legal responsibility (obey the law), Ethical responsibility (do what's right and fair even beyond legal requirements), and Discretionary/Philanthropic responsibility (be a good corporate citizen — charity, volunteering).

Exam tipCarroll's pyramid order is a common exam point: Economic sits at the base as the foundation everything else rests on — a company can't be ethical or philanthropic if it isn't profitable and viable first.

Milton Friedman (1970) gave the strongest economic argument against CSR: business's only responsibility is to make a profit for its owners while obeying the law — social problems belong to government, not business. Related objections include the competitive argument (internalising social costs disadvantages a firm against less scrupulous competitors) and the capability argument (executives are trained in finance and operations, not solving societal problems). Arguments in favour include the self-interest case (investing in society today forestalls tougher regulation tomorrow), the resource argument (large corporations have the capital to make a real difference), and growing stakeholder pressure that makes social responsiveness a practical necessity.

Stakeholders are individuals or groups affected by an organisation's policies and actions. Primary stakeholders have a direct stake — shareholders, employees, customers, business partners, communities. Secondary stakeholders are affected without a direct stake — government, regulatory bodies, media, and competitors. Contemporary CSR issues span environmental concerns (pollution, waste, global warming), global/labour issues ('sweatshop' conditions, child labour), and technology issues (data privacy, genetic engineering).
recap:
• CSR = strategic integration of social/environmental concern into business, not just charity. Triple Bottom Line: profit, people, planet.
  • Carroll's pyramid: Economic (foundation) → Legal → Ethical → Discretionary/Philanthropic.
  • Against CSR: Friedman's economic argument, the competitive argument, the capability argument.
  • For CSR: self-interest (avoids future regulation), resource argument, stakeholder pressure.
  • Primary stakeholders: shareholders, employees, customers. Secondary: government, regulators, media, competitors.
  • Contemporary issues: environmental, global/labour (sweatshops, child labour), technology (privacy, biotech).

quiz.q: According to Bowen (1953), social responsibility was first defined as:
opts: A government tax imposed on large corporations
A synonym for maximising shareholder profit only
The set of moral and personal obligations an employer must follow, considering policies/decisions in terms of society's objectives and values
A purely legal requirement with no moral dimension

quiz.q: ISO 26000 (2010) defines social responsibility as an organisation's responsibility for the impacts of its decisions and activities on:
opts: Only its direct competitors
Only its own employees exclusively
Society and the environment, through transparent and ethical behaviour
Only its own shareholders, with no wider consideration

quiz.q: The 'Triple Bottom Line' concept in CSR is commonly summarised by the slogan:
opts: Profit, people, planet
Profit, price, promotion
Growth, greed, glory
People, product, place

quiz.q: CSR is distinguished from mere charity or philanthropy because CSR:
opts: Is identical in every respect to charity
Never involves any donation of resources
Encompasses a strategic approach to business management extending beyond isolated giving
Is required only of non-profit organisations

quiz.q: According to the chapter, the phrase 'Corporate Social Responsibility' has been in wide use since approximately:
opts: The 1800s
The 2020s only
The 1400s
The 1960s

quiz.q: The philosophy known as 'Social Darwinism', practised by many late-19th-century business tycoons, justified:
opts: Cutthroat, even brutal, competitive strategies with little concern for social impact
Extensive corporate philanthropy as standard company policy
Government ownership of all industry
Strict environmental regulation of business

quiz.q: The Sherman Antitrust Act is cited in the chapter as an example of:
opts: Early 20th-century backlash against the power and antisocial practices of big business
A stakeholder engagement framework
A modern CSR reporting standard
A treaty governing international trade tariffs

quiz.q: Environmental Accountability, as a type of CSR, includes practices such as:
opts: Increasing the use of non-recyclable materials
Minimising pollution, greenhouse gas emissions and waste production
Avoiding any renewable energy investment
Ignoring all environmental impact entirely

quiz.q: Ethical Responsibility, as a type of CSR, focuses on:
opts: Ignoring supplier diversity entirely
Ensuring the organisation operates in a just and moral manner toward all stakeholders
Only maximising short-term profit with no ethical consideration
Avoiding all forms of investor disclosure

quiz.q: Philanthropic Responsibility, as a type of CSR, refers to:
opts: A synonym for economic responsibility with no distinction
Only actions required by government regulation
How a company uses its resources to make the world a better place, such as charitable donations
A legally mandated tax payment

quiz.q: According to Carroll and Buchholtz's (2003) four-part CSR definition, which of the following is one of the four dimensions?
opts: Economic, Legal, Ethical, and Discretionary responsibilities
Only Economic responsibility
Only Legal and Ethical responsibilities
Only Discretionary responsibility

quiz.q: Milton Friedman (1970) is closely associated with which argument regarding CSR?
opts: The Triple Bottom Line concept
The stakeholder theory of CSR
The economic argument against CSR, holding that business's primary responsibility is to make a profit for owners while obeying the law
The strongest argument in favour of extensive corporate philanthropy

quiz.q: The 'Competitive' argument against CSR holds that:
opts: CSR always improves a firm's competitive position with no downside
Internalising the costs of socially responsible action places a firm at a competitive disadvantage relative to firms that do not
CSR has no relationship to a firm's costs whatsoever
Only government-owned firms can practise CSR

quiz.q: The 'Capability' argument against CSR suggests that:
opts: CSR should be mandatory for every single firm regardless of size
All business executives are perfectly equipped to solve any social problem
Only government can ever generate any profit
Business executives are typically trained in finance/marketing/operations, not in solving complex societal problems

quiz.q: The 'Self-Interest' (long-run survival) argument in favour of CSR suggests that:
opts: CSR has no long-term benefit to a corporation whatsoever
Government regulation is entirely unrelated to CSR practices
CSR is purely an act of charity with no strategic value
Investing in society today can forestall future government regulation and secure a favourable long-term operating environment

quiz.q: According to Post, Lawrence and Weber, stakeholders are best described as:
opts: Only the organisation's direct competitors
Only the organisation's direct shareholders
Only government regulatory bodies
Individuals and groups that are affected by an organisation's policies, procedures and actions

quiz.q: Which of the following is classified as a PRIMARY stakeholder, according to Carroll and Buchholtz (2003)?
opts: Special Interest Groups
Shareholders (Owners), Employees and Customers
Local, State and Federal Government
The Media

quiz.q: Which of the following is classified as a SECONDARY stakeholder?
opts: Shareholders (Owners)
Regulatory Bodies and Competitors
Customers
Employees

quiz.q: Which of the following is identified as a contemporary global CSR issue relating to labour standards?
opts: Only issues related to executive compensation
Only issues related to shareholder dividend policy
Only domestic issues with no international relevance
Concerns over 'sweatshop' conditions and child labour in overseas manufacturing plants

quiz.q: Technology-related CSR issues discussed in the chapter include concerns over:
opts: Internet privacy, data security, and biotechnology issues such as genetic engineering
Only issues related to office furniture procurement
Only issues related to postal mail delivery
Only issues unrelated to any ethical consideration
